old.name: Bandol Rouge (Mourvèdre)
old.hook: The one Var wine built to age like a serious red, because the appellation forces it to: at least 50% Mourvèdre, and eighteen months' ageing - much of it in old-oak foudre - before release. Late-ripening Mourvèdre only finishes fully in this sea-facing amphitheatre of limestone terraces (Pibarnon climbs to 300m), which is why no other French appellation is built around it. Young, it drinks of leather, garrigue and black olive more than fruit; decant it.

old_also.name: Bandol
old_also.text: The Var's glory and the reason to take the region seriously. Mourvedre-led (minimum 50%), the reds are aged at least 18 months in large old oak foudres — tannic and closed young, built to run for decades. AOC since 1941. Domaine Tempier (the Peyraud family; farm since 1834) and Chateau de Pibarnon (vines on hand-built restanque terraces in a natural amphitheatre of blue marl) are the references. The rose is serious too — the one Provence pink genuinely worth cellaring a year.

old.name: Bandol Rosé
old.hook: Not the pale poolside kind. Tempier's rosé runs roughly 55% Mourvèdre - darker and structured, built for bouillabaisse rather than sunbathing. It was Domaine Tempier, carried to America by importer Kermit Lynch from the late 1970s, that taught drinkers a Provençal rosé could be a serious wine. Treat it like a light red: it takes fish soup, aïoli, even lamb.

old_also.name: Provence rose (the machine)
old_also.text: The caveat, told straight: Provence is the world's rose engine (about 40-45% of France's AOP rose, ~5% of global rose), and Sacha Lichine's Whispering Angel made pale pink a luxury category worth over a billion euros a year. Much of it is fashion, priced above reds of more substance. Drink it young, cold and local — but don't mistake the colour for the region's real depth, which is in Bandol.

old.name: Côtes de Provence Rosé
old.hook: The everyday Var pour, and an industry: rosé is around 80% of the appellation's output, mostly Grenache-Cinsault-Syrah pressed pale and bone-dry. Drink the most recent vintage, cold and young - it is not built to keep, and last year's bottle is already tiring.

old_also.name: Cotes de Provence
old_also.text: The workhorse and the volume: the largest Provencal appellation, roughly 20,000 hectares, about 90% of it rose (Grenache, Cinsault, Syrah, Rolle). Quality runs from industrial to genuinely fine. Its cooler inland sibling, Coteaux Varois en Provence around Brignoles, is often the better value.

old.name: Pastis
old.hook: The 6pm ritual, not a wine. Star anise, liquorice and garrigue herbs, cut roughly five parts cold water to one until it louches milky - water first, then ice, so the anethole doesn't clump. It is not made in the Var: Ricard is Marseille's child, created there in 1932 amid the wave of pastis that filled the void left by the 1915 absinthe ban. Reach for Henri Bardouin, built on more than sixty plants and spices, if you want to taste the herbs past the liquorice.

old.name: Fleur de Figue (fig liqueur)
old.hook: The Var's other obsession is the fig - the violet Bourjassotte Noire of Solliès-Pont, France's only AOP fig. This liqueur, macerated and bottled in the Var at Taradeau, is September in a glass: a digestif, or splashed into cold rosé or sparkling wine as an apéritif. Real fruit, none of the synthetic fig-candy note.

old.name: Liqueur de châtaigne / Crème de marrons (Collobrières)
old.hook: Collobrières, deep in the Massif des Maures, is the chestnut capital of the coast, its wooded slopes long planted with châtaigneraies. The Confiserie Azuréenne - making marrons glacés since 1945 - turns the chestnut into everything, alcohol included, alongside its celebrated crème de marrons. Autumn drinking; the village chestnut festival fills the last three Sundays of October.

old.name: Superbuvette
old.label: Toulon (Rue des Arts quarter
old.hook: The clearest expression of living-wine culture in the Var: a vintage-furnished neighbourhood cave-bar pouring only natural and 'living' wines, plus a short vegetal plate — seasonal dips, a vinegar-marinated hard-boiled egg, local cheese and olives. Terrace, no pretension.

bars:Les Quilles.group: Natural wine, three counters in Toulon

old.name: Les Quilles
old.label: Toulon (6 Place d'Armes)
old.hook: A tiny 30 m² cave whose whole point is the person behind the counter and a tightly-chosen natural list that leans into local Var growers (carignan, grenache) and Bandol reds. The kind of place where you buy one bottle and leave with three recommendations; an adjoining bistro, Le Pas de Côté, sits alongside.

old.name: La Dégust' Nature
old.label: Toulon (48 Cours Lafayette
old.hook: Caviste-and-bar on Toulon's great Provençal market street — pull up on a stool among the stalls, drink something low-intervention from a 300-plus natural list, eat charcuterie, cheese or a vegetarian spread. The owner genuinely knows the natural canon.

old.name: Bar du Sube
old.hook: A first-floor balcony bar with the oldest terrace in town, looking straight down the working port.
old.text: A first-floor balcony bar with the oldest terrace in town, looking straight down the working port. The Sube is the anti-Byblos: a modest, centuries-old three-star hotel right on the quay whose first-floor balcony is said to be the oldest in Saint-Tropez, and whose bar is a front-row seat on the endless choreography of yachts and sailing boats coming and going. Its five small terrace tables are the most fought-over in town. Climb higher and there is an English bar of mahogany and model boats, with a fireplace, subdued light and Art Deco panelling, a sailors' snug that nods to the town's 'Les Voiles' regatta rather than any nightclub. The real thing: for the price of one drink you get the single best free theatre on the port, from a perch that predates every palace on the peninsula. Signal Historic 3-star port hotel; oldest balcony in town over the harbour; mahogany English/Art Deco bar above

old.name: Terrasse de la Villa Belrose
old.hook: A panoramic terrace bar high in the Gassin hills for a glass of rosé over the whole bay.
old.text: A panoramic terrace bar high in the Gassin hills for a glass of rosé over the whole bay. The genius of the Althoff Villa Belrose is altitude and distance: it sits five minutes but a whole world away from the Saint-Tropez crush, on a Gassin hillside where the terrace hangs above the roadstead and the pool. You come here not for a scene but for the oldest ritual on this coast, a cold glass of Provence rosé while the light goes long over the gulf and the yachts below shrink to toys. The gastronomy carries a real name, chef Jimmy Coutel's 'Le Belrose' (Coutel has led the kitchen since 2022), but the terrace apéritif is the point. The real thing: this is a Leading Hotel of the World that trades entirely on the view, and it closes for winter, so the drink is a summer-season pleasure. Signal Leading Hotels of the World; reopened 24 April 2026 for the season, closes for winter; chef Jimmy Coutel since 2022

old.name: Bar Le Soleil d'Eau — Château de la Messardière
old.hook: A terrace aperitif at a fairy-tale hilltop château-palace above the town.
old.text: A terrace aperitif at a fairy-tale hilltop château-palace above the town. The Messardière is a 19th-century folly with turrets, domes and arcades, built as a wedding gift from cognac merchant Gabriel Dupuy d'Angeac to his daughter Louise and her husband, cavalry officer Henry Brisson de La Messardière, and perched in a 25-acre park of umbrella pines and cypress above Saint-Tropez. It joined the Airelles collection in 2019 and reopened as a palace in July 2021; the drink to take is on the terrace of the Bar Le Soleil d'Eau, aperitif in hand, with the Gulf of Saint-Tropez laid out below and the pine-resin heat all around. The real thing: this is the largest hotel in Saint-Tropez, yet its pleasure is the oldest and simplest, height, shade, and a slow glass while the bay turns gold. Signal 19th-century château (wedding gift, Dupuy d'Angeac family); Airelles Collection since 2019, reopened as palace July 2021

old.name: La Réserve à la Plage
old.text: The quiet-luxury answer to the party clubs, opened in 2019 as the beach arm of the five-star hotel La Réserve Ramatuelle. Owner Michel Reybier had Philippe Starck design a deliberately understated, bohemian-chic cabana, with a Mediterranean sharing menu overseen by Eric Canino, chef of the group's Michelin-starred restaurant La Voile. The honest truth Calm and design-led rather than a scene — which you pay handsomely for. This is a serious restaurant on the sand, priced accordingly, not a place to dance on the tables. Signal Opened 2019; Michel Reybier hotel group, interiors by Philippe Starck, cuisine under Eric Canino. Open for 2026 (roughly late April to early October).

old.name: Loulou / Moorea
old.text: Moorea is old Pampelonne — a beach that traces its roots back some seventy years to a bamboo straw hut with a barbecue and a few mattresses. Loulou, opened in 2019 by the Loulou Group, brought the glossy new-era 'art de vivre' concept to the same stretch, its name and 1950s-Riviera styling an homage to Loulou de la Falaise, Yves Saint Laurent's muse. The honest truth Loulou is firmly in the see-and-be-seen tier: designer crowd, high sunbed and dining minimums. The romance of Moorea's simple-hut origins is long gone from the prices. Signal Loulou opened 2019 (Loulou Group), named for YSL muse Loulou de la Falaise; Moorea one of Pampelonne's oldest beaches. Both open for 2026 (Loulou 23/04–03/10; Moorea 01/05–30/10).

old.name: Nikki Beach
old.text: The blueprint of the modern daytime-party beach club. The Miami brand chose Pampelonne for its second outpost, opening in summer 2002 with a grand-opening party still talked about on the strip. It set the template of DJ, pool, magnums and dancing-on-the-daybeds that much of Pampelonne now copies. The site was fully renovated in 2024, and from July 2026 its restaurant operates under a new name, Maurice à la Plage, while the venue itself stays open as Nikki Beach. The honest truth The champagne-spray, bottle-service archetype — loud, expensive and crowd-pleasing rather than discreet. Expect daybed minimums and a table spend that climbs fast once the music does. Signal Opened summer 2002 as the brand's first location outside Miami Beach; renovated 2024, restaurant rebranded 'Maurice à la Plage' for the 2026 season.

old.name: Les Caves du Roy — Hôtel Byblos
old.hook: The legendary cellar nightclub-bar inside the Byblos, open only in season.
old.text: The legendary cellar nightclub-bar inside the Byblos, open only in season. The whole hotel is a love letter to a muse: Lebanese businessman Jean-Prosper Gay-Para built the Byblos as a 'palace of a thousand and one nights' inspired by Brigitte Bardot, a faux-Provençal hamlet in apricot and salmon stucco inaugurated on 27 May 1967 with godmothers Bardot and Mireille Darc and three days of festivities for more than 700 guests. Its cellar-bar, Les Caves du Roy, has been the 'temple of Tropezian nights' since July 1967, with Juliette Gréco, Françoise Sagan and Jacques Chazot at the opening and Mick and Bianca Jagger's wedding celebrated here in 1971. Gay-Para lost the hotel within months, selling to Sylvain Floirat on 19 September 1967 after the Six-Day War pulled him back to Beirut; the Floirat family has kept the flame for over fifty years. The real thing: the legend is deliberately rationed, weekends only in spring and autumn and nightly only across high summer, roughly late June to end of August. Signal Byblos inaugurated 27 May 1967; Caves du Roy open since July 1967; seasonal, nightly late Jun-late Aug (2026)

old_also.name: Les Caves du Roy
old_also.text: The legendary nightclub of Saint-Tropez, in the basement of the Hôtel Byblos. It opened in July 1967 — the Byblos was built by Lebanese businessman Jean-Prosper Gay-Para, the story goes, in tribute to Bardot — with a three-night launch stage-managed by Jacqueline Veyssière and guests including Juliette Gréco and Françoise Sagan. It has set the tone of Tropézien nights ever since. The honest truth The door is the whole experience, and it is famously selective. There is no real cover so much as an unspoken table minimum, and champagne is sold by the magnum at prices designed to thin the crowd. Signal Opened July 1967 in the Hôtel Byblos; running as the town's marquee club ever since. Open for 2026 (Byblos reopens 22 April; nightly from late June to late August).
